nodes.summary: For every vertex set $X$ of a finite graph $G$, $\rho_G(V \setminus X) = \rho_G(X)$: the two cut matrices are transposes of each other, because adjacency is symmetric.
nodes.title: Cut-rank is symmetric

nodes.summary: If $H$ is locally equivalent to $G$, then $\rho_H(X) = \rho_G(X)$ for every vertex set $X$.
nodes.title: Locally equivalent graphs have the same cut-rank function

nodes.summary: For every finite graph $G$ and vertex sets $X, Y$, The source deduces it from the submodular inequality for ranks of submatrices, $\mathrm{rk}\,M[X_1, Y_1] + \mathrm{rk}\,M[X_2, Y_2] \ge \mathrm{rk}\,M[X_1 \cup X_2, Y_1 \cap Y_2] + \mathrm{rk}\,M[X_1 \cap X_2, Y_1 \cup Y_2]$ (its Proposition 6.1), applied to the adjacency matrix.
nodes.title: Cut-rank is submodular

nodes.summary: For every finite simple graph $G$, every vertex $v$ and every vertex set $X$, The proof follows the source. By symmetry of cut-rank we may assume $v \in X$. Then the cut matrix of $G * v$ is obtained from that of $G$ by adding the row of $v$ to the rows of the neighbours of $v$ in $X$; this is left multiplication by an invertible matrix (it squares to the identity over $\mathrm{GF}(2)$), so the rank does not…
nodes.title: Local complementation preserves the cut-rank function

nodes.summary: In a complete graph every cut matrix is an all-ones matrix, of rank at most one. Hence $\rho_{K_V}(X) \le 1$ for every vertex set $X$, and complete graphs have rank-width at most one, although $K_n$ has tree-width $n - 1$.
nodes.title: Complete graphs have cut-rank at most one

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a finite simple graph. For a vertex set $X$, the cut-rank $\rho_G(X)$ is the rank over the two-element field $\mathrm{GF}(2)$ of the $X \times (V \setminus X)$ matrix whose $(x, y)$ entry is $1$ when $x$ and $y$ are adjacent and $0$ otherwise. In particular $\rho_G(\emptyset) = \rho_G(V) = 0$, and $\rho_G(\{v\}) \le 1$.
nodes.title: Cut-rank function

nodes.summary: Fix $k$. A $k$-expression builds a graph whose vertices carry labels in $\{1, \dots, k\}$ (here `Fin k`) from
nodes.title: Graphs generated by `k`-expressions

nodes.summary: For every finite graph $G$, $\mathrm{cw}(G) \le 2^{\mathrm{rw}(G) + 1} - 1$: a graph of rank-width at most $k$ has clique-width at most $2^{k+1} - 1$. With the inequality $\mathrm{rw}(G) \le \mathrm{cw}(G)$, a class of graphs has bounded rank-width if and only if it has bounded clique-width. The source's proof builds a $(2^{k+1} - 1)$-expression bottom-up along a rooted rank-decomposition, using that a matrix of…
nodes.title: Clique-width is bounded by an exponential in rank-width (Oum–Seymour)

nodes.summary: A graph with exactly one vertex has clique-width at most one: it is the value of the $1$-expression $\cdot_1$.
nodes.title: A single vertex has clique-width at most one

nodes.summary: A graph has clique-width at most $k$ if it has no vertices or some vertex labelling of it is generated by a $k$-expression. The clique-width $\mathrm{cw}(G)$ is the least such $k$. Complete graphs on at least two vertices have clique-width $2$, and every graph on $n$ vertices has clique-width at most $n$.
nodes.title: Clique-width at most `k`

nodes.summary: For every finite graph $G$, $\mathrm{rw}(G) \le \mathrm{cw}(G)$: a graph of clique-width at most $k$ has rank-width at most $k$. The source's proof reads a rank-decomposition off the parse tree of a $k$-expression; across each edge of the tree the vertices on one side fall into at most $k$ label classes with identical neighbourhoods on the other side, so the cut matrix has at most $k$ distinct rows.
nodes.title: Rank-width is at most clique-width (Oum–Seymour)

nodes.summary: If $H$ is a vertex-minor of a finite graph $G$ and $G$ has rank-width at most $k$, then so does $H$. The source's proof: local complementation does not change the cut-rank function, and deleting a vertex does not increase cut-rank, so a rank-decomposition of $G$ restricts to one of $H$ of no larger width.
nodes.title: Rank-width does not increase under vertex-minors

nodes.summary: Let $k \ge 1$. A finite graph $G$ has rank-width at most $k$ if and only if every vertex-minor of $G$ with at most $(6^{k+1} - 1)/5$ vertices has rank-width at most $k$.
nodes.title: Excluded vertex-minors for bounded rank-width (Oum)

nodes.summary: If $H$ is locally equivalent to $G$, then $H$ has rank-width at most $k$ exactly when $G$ does; that is, locally equivalent graphs have the same rank-width.
nodes.title: Locally equivalent graphs have the same rank-width

nodes.summary: For every finite graph $G$, vertex $v$ and natural number $k$, the graph $G * v$ has rank-width at most $k$ if and only if $G$ does. Indeed every rank-decomposition has the same width for both graphs, since their cut-rank functions agree.
nodes.title: Local complementation preserves rank-width

nodes.summary: A graph with at most one vertex has rank-width at most every $k$, that is, rank-width $0$.
nodes.title: Graphs with at most one vertex have rank-width zero

nodes.summary: A finite graph of tree-width at most $k$ has rank-width at most $k + 1$. The converse fails: complete graphs have rank-width at most one but unbounded tree-width.
nodes.title: Rank-width is at most tree-width plus one

nodes.summary: A finite graph $G$ has rank-width at most $k$ if it has at most one vertex or it has a rank-decomposition of width at most $k$. The rank-width $\mathrm{rw}(G)$ is the least such $k$, with $\mathrm{rw}(G) = 0$ for graphs with at most one vertex as in the sources.
nodes.title: Rank-width at most `k`

nodes.summary: A rank-decomposition $(T, L)$ has width at most $k$ for a graph $G$ if every edge $ij$ of $T$ has width at most $k$, the width of $ij$ being the cut-rank of its side. By symmetry of cut-rank either side gives the same width.
nodes.title: Width at most `k`

nodes.summary: For every vertex $v$, the local complement $G * v$ is a vertex-minor of $G$.
nodes.title: Local complementation gives a vertex-minor

nodes.summary: A graph $H$ is a vertex-minor of a graph $G$ if $H$ is isomorphic to an induced subgraph of a graph locally equivalent to $G$. Equivalently, $H$ is obtained from $G$ by a sequence of local complementations and vertex deletions; the source introduces the relation in this second form.
nodes.title: Vertex-minor

nodes.summary: The neighbours of $v$ in $G * v$ are exactly its neighbours in $G$: local complementation at $v$ changes only edges between two neighbours of $v$.
nodes.title: Local complementation keeps the neighbourhood of its vertex

nodes.summary: Distinct vertices $x, y$ are adjacent in $G * v$ if and only if "$x$ and $y$ are adjacent in $G$" differs from "$x$ and $y$ are both neighbours of $v$ in $G$".
nodes.title: Adjacency after local complementation

nodes.summary: Local complementation at a vertex is an involution: $G * v * v = G$.
nodes.title: Local complementation is an involution

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a simple graph and $v$ a vertex. The local complementation of $G$ at $v$ is the graph $G * v$ on the same vertices in which two distinct vertices $x, y$ are adjacent exactly when either $xy$ is an edge of $G$ or both $x$ and $y$ are neighbours of $v$, but not both: In words, the subgraph induced on the neighbourhood of $v$ is replaced by its complement; the edges at $v$ are unchanged.
nodes.title: Local complementation

nodes.summary: Two simple graphs on the same vertex set are locally equivalent if one is obtained from the other by a finite sequence of local complementations. Since each local complementation is an involution, this is an equivalence relation.
nodes.title: Locally equivalent graphs

nodes.summary: If a graph has rank-width at most $k$ and $k \le l$, it has rank-width at most $l$.
nodes.title: Rank-width bounds are monotone

nodes.summary: A rank-decomposition of width at most $k$ for a graph has width at most $l$ for every $l \ge k$.
nodes.title: Width bounds are monotone

nodes.summary: A rank-decomposition of a finite vertex set $V$ is a pair $(T, L)$ of a finite tree $T$ in which every node has degree one or three and a bijection $L$ from $V$ onto the leaves of $T$. It does not depend on a graph; a graph enters only through the width of the decomposition.
nodes.title: Rank-decomposition

nodes.summary: Every graph is a vertex-minor of itself.
nodes.title: Every graph is a vertex-minor of itself

nodes.summary: Deleting an edge $ij$ of the decomposition tree $T$ splits the leaves into two parts. The side of $(i, j)$ is the set of vertices whose leaves lie in the component containing $i$; the side of $(j, i)$ is the rest of the vertex set.
nodes.title: Side of a tree edge

nodes.summary: If $H$ is locally equivalent to $G$, then $G$ is locally equivalent to $H$, because each local complementation undoes itself.
nodes.title: Local equivalence is symmetric

can_prove.label: ready to prove
can_prove.meaning: Statement is in Lean and nothing it needs is blocked, so the proof can start.

can_state.label: ready to state
can_state.meaning: Everything its statement uses is in Lean, so the statement can be written in Lean.

conditional.label: conditionally proved
conditional.meaning: Proof compiles, but rests on an open statement without a recorded Lean proof.

fully_proved.label: fully proved
fully_proved.meaning: Proved, and every prerequisite is fully proved too.

inventory_checked.label: inventory checked
inventory_checked.meaning: Module inventory checked in full; it records inspection, not a mathematical proof.

inventory_pending.label: inventory pending
inventory_pending.meaning: Module inventory not yet checked in full; it records inspection, not a mathematical proof.

not_ready.label: not ready
not_ready.meaning: Needs more blueprint work before it can be attempted.

proved.label: proved
proved.meaning: Proof compiles, but something it rests on is not finished.

stated.label: statement formalized
stated.meaning: Statement is in Lean; the proof is not.
